pages.text: Every fluid in the plant is a real one, with its real density, viscosity, freezing and boiling point and flash point; goggles on a pipe, pump, valve, tank or basin give them. Water-based fluids freeze in the pipe: below the freezing point a pipe holds still and a pump moves nothing until the heat comes back.
pages.title: Liquid properties

pages.text: Water freezes at 0 °C, seawater at -1.9, brines and acids far lower.

A fluid past its boiling point in an open basin, with no mixer or press over it, boils off 25 mB every 2 seconds, and whatever it carries is breathed: acid fumes, poison, nickel carbonyl. In a pipe or tank the goggles warn instead. Fresh Bayer liquor leaves the digester at 145 °C under pressure, too hot for plastic pipe.

A flammable fluid let out by a burst pipe past its flash point beside a flame, lava or a burner, or anywhere past its autoignition temperature, catches fire; nickel carbonyl ignites at 60 °C. Spilt oils and fuels in the world burn as wood does, the lower the flash point the readier.

Thick fluids pump slower, as the Hydraulic Institute's correction has a pump lose flow past about 100 mPa·s: heavy oil at 3,000 mPa·s goes at about half, and a polymer melt or fresh concrete no slower than a quarter.

Each line of the table gives density in kg/m³, viscosity in mPa·s, and freezing to boiling point in °C, then the flash point and hazards. Gases are at 20 °C and 1 atm and hot melts at their own temperature; an oil's freezing point is its pour point.
